nutshell: Existing point-tracking benchmarks (e.g. TAP-Vid-DAVIS) use mostly smooth third-person camera motion where tracked points rarely leave the frame, but egocentric (head-mounted camera) video has frequent, fast motion that pushes objects and scene regions out of view and back in. This paper introduces EgoPoints, a benchmark of manually annotated egocentric point tracks emphasizing out-of-view and re-identification (ReID) cases, shows every current SOTA point tracker degrades sharply on it, and proposes K-EPIC, a semi-real synthetic training pipeline for fine-tuning trackers to be better at exactly this failure mode.
contributions: EgoPoints benchmark: 517 sequences / 4,703 sparsely annotated point tracks from EPIC-KITCHENS-100, deliberately curated (via VISOR hand annotations and EPIC Fields 3D point clouds) to contain 9x more out-of-view points and 59x more re-identification points than TAP-Vid-DAVIS, with new metrics (delta*_avg, ReIDdelta_avg, in-view accuracy, out-of-view accuracy) that separate ordinary tracking accuracy from out-of-view detection and re-identification specifically.

A systematic diagnosis of current SOTA trackers' failure modes on egocentric video: benchmarking 5 models shows large accuracy drops versus DAVIS (e.g. CoTracker 74.7 -> 38.5 on delta_avg) and near-total ReID failure (0-15%), and identifies two distinct failure patterns - models that simply keep points pinned in-view (near-zero out-of-view accuracy, e.g. BootsTAPIR, LocoTrack) versus models that correctly detect points leaving view but fail to re-acquire them on return (CoTracker).

K-EPIC: a pipeline generating 11K semi-real training sequences by combining real static scene points (extracted from EPIC Fields camera poses/point clouds, filtered using a pretrained CoTracker as a consistency check) with synthetic dynamic 3D object points from TAP-Vid-Kubric, plus a cheap 'looped' frame-reordering augmentation that returns objects to their starting position specifically to force re-identification supervision during fine-tuning.
deficiencies: Even after fine-tuning, absolute re-identification performance stays very poor - the paper's own best result is ReIDdelta_avg = 16.8% (Table 3), meaning over 80% of re-identification cases still fail; the paper's own Limitations section concedes this, so K-EPIC is a small mitigation of the problem the benchmark exposes, not a solution to it.

Fine-tuning is only evaluated on 2 of the 5 baseline models from the initial benchmark comparison (PIPs++ and CoTracker), explicitly due to stated 'time constraints' - the more recent, stronger models that failed most catastrophically on ReID in Table 2 (LocoTrack, CoTracker v3, BootsTAPIR, at 0.0-15.0% ReID accuracy) are never tested with the proposed fix, so it's unclear whether K-EPIC helps the current best trackers or is specific to the two older architectures chosen.

The benchmark itself is annotated by a single expert annotator with no inter-annotator agreement or reliability analysis reported, and averages only ~8.5 points per sequence (593 ReID tracks total) - the paper draws model-comparison conclusions from binary accuracy metrics on this benchmark without reporting any variance or confidence intervals.

K-EPIC's dynamic object motion (rotation/translation/collisions) is borrowed wholesale from TAP-Vid-Kubric's generic synthetic 24-frame sequences with no semantic connection to the egocentric kitchen scenes it's composited onto - only the static background points are actually egocentric-derived, which limits how much of any ReID improvement is genuinely 'egocentric' learning versus generic occlusion/reappearance pattern-matching.
notable: The 'looped' sequence augmentation - reordering K-EPIC frames as [1,3,5,...,24,22,...,2] so an object returns to its exact starting position - is a simple, cheap way to manufacture re-identification supervision without any additional real annotation; a reusable trick for other domains that lack real re-appearance examples. Also worth flagging: references [38] and [39] are the same EPIC Fields paper cited twice, once as a NeurIPS 2024 entry and once as NeurIPS 2023, with a co-author name spelled two different ways (Iro Laina vs. Iro Larina) between the two - likely a preprint/camera-ready duplication artifact rather than two distinct works, consistent with the duplicate-citation pattern seen elsewhere in this batch of papers.
